strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in open-vocabulary 3D scene-graph construction: erroneous multi-view aggregation caused by occlusion and poor viewpoints.
The proposed pipeline is coherent, combining adaptive point-cloud downsampling, rendered best-view observations, caption-consistency-based uncertainty estimation, and contextual caption refinement.

Human evaluation on eight Replica scenes reports substantial node-precision gains over ConceptGraphs (0.82 versus 0.68) while producing more valid objects and fewer duplicates. Edge precision also improves to 0.91.

The component ablations show consistent degradation when re-shot views, retrieval, or concatenated visual inputs are removed. The random-retrieval comparison provides some evidence that spatial context is useful.
The dynamic voxel-size rule is simple and practically motivated. The reported mapping-time reduction from 6.65 to 2.49 seconds per iteration is potentially valuable.
The method and qualitative examples are generally understandable, and the appendix provides pseudocode, per-scene ablation results, rendered-view examples, and a useful failure-motivation case study.
weaknesses: The experimental scope is narrow for an Algorithms/General contribution: all results use only eight scenes from the synthetic Replica dataset. There is no evaluation on real RGB-D data, other 3D benchmarks, noisy camera poses/depth, or downstream navigation and manipulation, despite motivating the work through real-world and safety-critical robotics.

The principal human evaluation lacks essential methodological information: number of annotators and judgments, agreement statistics, adjudication procedure, exact sampling counts, masking of method identity, and confidence intervals or significance tests. Consequently, the large reported precision gains are difficult to assess reliably.

Baseline comparability is insufficiently established. The proposed method changes mapping, node captioning, graph connectivity, relation vocabulary, prompts, and foundation-model use simultaneously. It is unclear whether ConceptGraphs and CG-D receive the same GPT models, inputs, prompts, and inference budget. Edge results are especially confounded by the expanded relation set and changed edge construction.

The claimed efficiency improvement concerns only one mapping measurement on Replica Room 0. End-to-end runtime, VLM/LLM latency, API cost, memory, point counts, and re-shot rendering cost are omitted; the added captioning and RAG calls may dominate overall execution. No controlled speed-accuracy curve compares dynamic and fixed downsampling over multiple voxel sizes and scenes.

The uncertainty mechanism is under-specified and unvalidated. The clustering algorithm applied to scalar caption-similarity scores and the meaning of the “top-1 cluster” are not defined, while the top-50% split is arbitrary. There is no calibration, error-detection AUROC, or correlation analysis showing that the score actually measures caption correctness. It also assumes that the re-shot caption is a reliable reference.

The object-level RAG contribution is relatively modest: it retrieves only the spatially nearest low-uncertainty caption. The paper calls this “semantic-aware retrieval,” although the described retriever is position-based, and it does not compare against stronger contextual alternatives such as multiple neighbors, scene-level context, or direct prompting without the RAG framing.

The semantic-segmentation ablation uses GPT-4o to assign generated captions to ground-truth categories, introducing evaluator dependence and possible bias because closely related proprietary models participate in generation. The assignment protocol may permit many-to-one matches and is not adequately specified or validated against human labels.

Table 2 provides little evidence for improved mapping quality: the mAcc gain over ConceptGraphs is only 0.04 points, f-mIoU is slightly worse, and several other methods have much higher f-mIoU. Results are imported from prior papers without demonstrating identical settings or reporting variability.

Important reproducibility details are deferred to a future code release, including k, the number and sampling of candidate viewpoints, clustering choices, prompts, background filtering, inference parameters, and random seeds. Reliance on proprietary, potentially changing or deprecated GPT endpoints further limits reproducibility.

The fusion score adds semantic and spatial terms in a [0,2] range but uses a threshold of 0.45. Since the normalized semantic term alone exceeds 0.45 for cosine similarity above -0.1, objects with negligible spatial overlap may be fused; the paper neither justifies this scale nor analyzes erroneous merges.

The ablations focus on node semantic segmentation and do not isolate the contributions to human-rated node and edge precision, dynamic downsampling, uncertainty ranking, or the expanded relation vocabulary. No repeated runs quantify stochastic variation from GPT inference.

Claims of improved robustness and suitability for safety-critical robotics are stronger than the evidence: no robustness stress tests, temporal/online experiments, uncertainty-aware abstention, or downstream task evaluation are presented. Overall, the idea is promising, but these evidence and specification gaps slightly favor rejection.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant computer-vision and robotics problem: reducing noisy multi-view object captions while accelerating open-vocabulary 3D scene-graph construction.
The proposed pipeline is conceptually coherent, combining scale-adaptive downsampling, rendered object views, caption-agreement-based uncertainty estimation, and contextual caption refinement.

On eight Replica scenes, the reported human-evaluated node precision improves from 0.68 for ConceptGraphs to 0.82, while edge precision rises from 0.82 to 0.91. The method also reports fewer duplicate objects and more valid nodes and edges.

The component ablations, per-scene results, qualitative examples, pseudocode, and explicit model identities provide useful supporting evidence. The reported reduction from 6.65 to 2.49 seconds per mapping iteration is practically promising.
weaknesses: No contribution type is declared, so I assess this as Algorithms/General. Under that standard, the evidence is too limited: all experiments use only eight scenes from the synthetic Replica dataset, with no real-world RGB-D sequences, cross-dataset evaluation, robustness tests, or downstream navigation/manipulation results despite the robotics and safety motivation.

The principal scene-graph comparison is restricted to ConceptGraphs and one variant. It is also confounded by changes in mapping, prompts, relation vocabulary, graph connectivity, and foundation models. The paper does not establish improvements under controlled, identical VLM/LLM backbones and prompts.

The human evaluation lacks essential information: annotator count, number of judgments per item, agreement, adjudication, detailed rubric, blinding, and confidence intervals. Precision plus raw valid-output counts does not measure graph recall or completeness, and the different edge vocabularies and graph densities further weaken comparability.

The central uncertainty estimator is not validated as an uncertainty measure. Agreement with a re-shot caption may reflect two correlated mistakes, while disagreement need not indicate that the crop caption is wrong. There are no calibration curves, error-detection AUROC, threshold analysis, or comparison with standard uncertainty/confidence baselines; clustering is also insufficiently specified.

The claimed RAG mechanism is quite weak and somewhat mischaracterized: it retrieves only the spatially nearest low-uncertainty object's caption rather than performing substantive semantic retrieval. The fixed top-50% split is arbitrary, and neighboring context could induce hallucinations. Sensitivity to this split and retrieval count is not evaluated.

The re-shot formulation makes assumptions that are not justified. Reconstructed object point clouds can remain incomplete or contaminated by segmentation errors, so rendering does not necessarily eliminate occlusion. The view-score weights and candidate sampling are not analyzed, and there are no comparisons against simpler view-selection strategies.

The dynamic scaling equations appear dimensionally inconsistent: a voxel size stated in meters is multiplied by the square root of a bounding-box diagonal measured in meters. The square-root rule is heuristic, and the claim that it avoids the accuracy-efficiency trade-off is unsupported by a runtime-quality curve, equal-point-budget baseline, or broad timing study. Hardware and end-to-end latency are also omitted.

The ablation evaluation uses GPT-4o as a semantic assigner, with insufficient prompt and matching details, introducing proprietary-model subjectivity and possible many-to-one assignment artifacts. It also produces an f-mIoU of 54.26 versus 35.65 in the main segmentation evaluation under a different protocol, making the quantitative story difficult to interpret.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate: code is only promised, several prompts and 'non-critical' hyperparameters are withheld, clustering and rendering details are incomplete, and proprietary API models introduce versioning and nondeterminism. Overall, the ideas have merit, but the evaluation and specification do not yet support the paper's broad accuracy, robustness, and practical-impact claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important failure mode in open-vocabulary 3D scene-graph construction: noisy multi-view captions caused by occlusion and unfavorable viewpoints. This is well motivated for embodied perception and robotics.

The proposed pipeline is coherent: reconstructed-object re-rendering provides cleaner views, caption agreement supplies an uncertainty proxy, nearby low-uncertainty objects provide contextual refinement, and scale-adaptive downsampling targets mapping efficiency.

Results on eight Replica scenes are promising. Average human-judged node precision improves from 0.68 for ConceptGraphs to 0.82, while edge precision improves from 0.82 to 0.91. The method also produces more valid nodes and edges with fewer duplicates.

The component ablations consistently indicate that re-shot views are the largest contributor and that spatially informed retrieval is preferable to random retrieval. The qualitative case study clearly illustrates the motivating occlusion problem.
Dynamic downsampling appears useful in practice: the reported mapping time decreases from 6.65 to 2.49 seconds per iteration while semantic-mapping accuracy remains comparable to ConceptGraphs.

The manuscript is generally understandable, provides equations, model identities, principal hyperparameters, pseudocode, qualitative visualizations, and a stated intention to release code. For the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the work offers a meaningful, if incremental, systems-level combination of ideas.
weaknesses: The evidence is limited to the synthetic Replica dataset. There is no evaluation on real RGB-D data, scenes outside the eight Replica environments, or an actual downstream navigation/manipulation task, despite claims concerning robustness and robotic utility. This substantially limits the demonstrated generality and impact.

The human evaluation is underspecified: the number of annotators, annotations per item, annotation counts, inter-annotator agreement, adjudication procedure, and confidence intervals are absent. Since this is the primary evidence for the headline node and edge gains, the omission prevents assessing statistical reliability.

The edge comparison is potentially confounded because the proposed method uses eight relation labels whereas ConceptGraphs uses five. The paper does not establish that edge candidate sets, relation coverage, prompts, and evaluation conditions are sufficiently matched for a controlled precision comparison. Recall or coverage against annotated ground truth is also missing.

Several important algorithmic choices are insufficiently defined or justified, including the clustering algorithm for caption similarities, what makes a cluster the 'top-1' cluster, the fixed 50% uncertainty split, candidate-view sampling, background filtering, and tie/failure handling. Referring unspecified prompts and parameters to a future code release weakens present reproducibility.

The uncertainty score is merely CLIP agreement with a VLM caption generated from the reconstructed view; it is neither calibrated nor evaluated as an uncertainty estimator. A confidently incorrect re-shot caption could corrupt both caption filtering and the low-uncertainty retrieval document. No uncertainty-quality curve, threshold sensitivity, or error-propagation analysis is provided.

The dynamic voxel rule is heuristic and dimensionally questionable: multiplying a voxel length by the square root of a bounding-box diagonal does not preserve length units. Its interaction with the similarly defined nearest-neighbor threshold is not analyzed, and there is no isolated accuracy/runtime ablation against other size-aware sampling rules.

The efficiency claim is supported only by one example for Replica room0. Hardware, measurement protocol, variability, memory, point counts, and end-to-end runtime—including rendering and repeated proprietary VLM/LLM calls—are not reported. Consequently, the paper establishes faster mapping rather than a faster complete 3DSG system.

The ablation evaluation relies on GPT-4o to assign predicted free-form captions to ground-truth classes, introducing a proprietary and potentially unstable evaluator without validation against human assignments. Its f-mIoU values also differ markedly from Table 2 because the assignment protocol changes, complicating interpretation; the aggregate values in Figure 3 are not transparently reconciled with the per-scene heatmaps in Figure 5.

The qualitative case study uses LLaVA, whereas the reported implementation uses GPT-4o-mini, so it is not clearly representative of the evaluated system. More systematic success and failure cases are needed.

Overall, the idea is appealing and the reported gains favor acceptance, but the limited benchmark scope, insufficiently controlled evaluation, and reproducibility gaps make this a borderline rather than confident acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical failure mode in open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs: inconsistent semantics caused by occlusion and limited viewpoints. The diagnose-then-rectify framing is intuitive and relevant to embodied vision.

The combination of virtual re-rendering, caption-consistency scoring, and context-based refinement is reasonably original as an Algorithms/General contribution. The method is modular and can use either an open-source VLM or GPT-4o.

Evaluation covers SceneFun3D, FunGraph3D, Replica, pose perturbations, and a physical robot demonstration. The human study reports substantial inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' kappa of 0.76), and the component ablations show sizeable improvements from re-shot verification.

Node results are promising: GPT-4o reaches 90.2 R@10 on SceneFun3D and 83.0 R@10 on FunGraph3D, while the LLaVA variant also improves several node metrics over OpenFunGraph. Human evaluation reports appreciably higher node and edge precision and fewer duplicate objects.
The method and motivation are generally presented clearly, with useful diagrams explaining the pipeline and view-selection criteria.
weaknesses: The central uncertainty estimator is insufficiently validated. Caption-to-caption CLIP similarity is treated as semantic uncertainty, but the paper reports no calibration, error-detection AUROC/AUPRC, correlation with correctness, or comparison against standard uncertainty and confidence baselines. Thus it is unclear whether the proposed score actually identifies erroneous nodes rather than merely linguistic disagreement.

Important implementation details are missing or ambiguous: the caption clustering algorithm, construction of the consensus caption and reliability score, top-k selection, prompts, dynamic nearest-neighbor ratio, association weighting, and edge-generation procedure are not fully specified. The dimensional interpretation of the adaptive voxel formula is also unclear. These omissions materially limit reproducibility.

The ablations do not isolate the main design choices adequately. There is no comparison with passive best-frame selection, random or maximum-visibility virtual views, direct multi-view prompting, alternative uncertainty measures, different anchor fractions, or multiple retrieved neighbors. The reported 'w/o Reshot' degradation therefore does not establish that the proposed scoring and uncertainty formulation are responsible for the gain.

The main benchmark gains are mixed. Edge improvements over OpenFunGraph are small or absent: Ours-GPT is worse at SceneFun3D R@5, improves R@10 by only 1.7 points, and merely ties FunGraph3D R@10; the LLaVA version is worse on all reported edge metrics. Several node gains are likewise modest. No confidence intervals, repeated runs, or significance tests are provided.

Fairness and robustness evidence are incomplete. Baselines use different foundation models and potentially different object-node inputs, while GPT-4o is presented as an upper-bound variant. The ablation evaluation additionally uses GPT-4o to map free-form predictions to labels, introducing a proprietary and potentially biased evaluator. The single pose-noise setting of 2 cm and 1 degree, without multiple seeds or a severity curve, does not justify describing the corruption as 'extreme.'

The proposed 'active' verification only re-renders an already reconstructed point cloud; it cannot recover unobserved surfaces, appearance, or texture, and the prior-view term explicitly favors previously observed directions. The paper overstates this as breaking dependence on finite observations and does not analyze failure cases involving incomplete or incorrectly fused geometry.

The robotic deployment is qualitative and apparently limited to one environment. It provides no scene-graph ground truth, downstream navigation/manipulation results, localization-noise measurements, repeated trials, or comparison with a baseline. Consequently, claims of deployment readiness, exceptional resilience, and hallucination-free graphs are not supported.

Runtime reporting covers only a selected mapping-stage number and approximate API cost. End-to-end latency, exact hardware for all variants, VLM calls per scene, memory use, and scaling with object or frame count are absent. Human-evaluation sample construction and blinding are also under-described. Overall, the idea is promising, but the evidence and specification leave a slight preference for rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: semantic inconsistency in open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs caused by occlusion and limited viewpoints. The diagnose-then-rectify organization is intuitive and potentially useful. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/88213b312ba94d9da70afdd520a01413/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The evaluation is broader than a minimal proof of concept, covering SceneFun3D, FunGraph3D, Replica, component ablations, pose perturbations, human judgments, and a physical robot demonstration.

Some empirical results are encouraging. Ours-GPT improves object R@10 from 87.8 to 90.2 on SceneFun3D and from 79.1 to 83.0 on FunGraph3D; the reported Replica human evaluation also shows sizable node- and edge-precision improvements over ConceptGraphs variants.
The manuscript is generally well organized, and the diagrams communicate the proposed pipeline and virtual-view scoring procedure clearly.
weaknesses: The central conceptual claim is overstated. A re-shot is rendered from a point cloud reconstructed from the same finite observations; it cannot reveal texture or geometry that was never captured, nor reliably resolve an object that remained occluded throughout the trajectory. Describing this as an unconstrained verification space or an active photographer that recovers true semantics is therefore misleading. It is better characterized as virtual view synthesis from existing evidence.

The proposed uncertainty is not validated as uncertainty. CLIP similarity between captions produced from two transformations of the same underlying observations measures self-consistency, not calibrated correctness. The paper provides no error-detection AUROC, calibration analysis, reliability diagram, or comparison with simple confidence/dispersion baselines. A confidently consistent but wrong caption would become a trusted RAG anchor and could propagate errors.

Core algorithmic details are missing: the dynamic nearest-neighbor ratio, association-score normalization, caption-clustering procedure, cluster-selection rule, consensus-caption construction, final reliability score, rendering process, and several thresholds are not formally specified. This prevents faithful reproduction and makes the technical contribution difficult to assess. The voxel-size equation also has unclear dimensional interpretation because it multiplies a quantity stated in meters by the square root of a length.

The main comparison does not isolate the contribution from model capacity. Ours-GPT uses GPT-4o, whereas the strongest baselines may use different captioning/reasoning models; there is no apples-to-apples baseline obtained by applying the original aggregation pipeline with the same GPT-4o prompts and inputs. Ours-LLaVA is slightly worse than OpenFunGraph on several SceneFun3D and edge metrics, while many GPT edge gains are marginal or absent—for example, FunGraph3D edge R@5 improves only from 65.1 to 65.7 and R@10 is tied at 91.4.

The ablations do not establish the claimed causal mechanism. They are performed only on Replica with a different evaluation pipeline, and removing re-shot processing changes both uncertainty estimation and visual input, rather than isolating uncertainty quality. There are no ablations for individual view-scoring terms, the top-50% anchor rule, number of retrieved neighbors, dynamic downsampling, or simple alternatives such as selecting the best observed crop.

Replica predictions are semantically assigned to ground truth using GPT-4o, which is also the model used by the strongest proposed variant. This creates a possible correlated evaluator/generator bias. Neither these results nor the main tables report uncertainty across runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite relatively small scene counts.

The robustness evidence does not justify terms such as “extreme,” “severe,” or “exceptional resilience.” Perturbations of 2 cm and 1 degree are modest, only one noise level is tested, and no repeated random trials or comparisons against baselines under the same corruption are provided. Moreover, the concatenated clean 2D crop can bypass a degraded re-shot, so the experiment does not directly validate robustness of the re-shot mechanism.

The real-world deployment is qualitative and apparently offline. It reports no number of runs, graph accuracy, localization error, runtime, failures, or improvement on an actual navigation/manipulation task. Consequently, claims of readiness for reliable or safety-critical robotics are unsupported. Total scene latency, VLM-query counts, memory use, and complete hardware-specific runtime are also missing.

The human-evaluation protocol remains underspecified: agreement is measured on only 100 units, no confidence intervals are reported, and the stated equivalence of “wooden table” and “brown desk” permits both category and attribute differences despite requiring correct semantic category and primary attributes. This weakens confidence in the reported precision advantage.

Overall, assessed as an Algorithms/General submission because no contribution type is declared, the paper has a plausible engineering idea and promising numbers, but the central interpretation, experimental controls, and reproducibility are not strong enough to support acceptance.

strengths: Assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution because no type is explicitly declared. The paper addresses an important failure mode in open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs: inconsistent semantics caused by occlusion and limited viewpoints.

The diagnose-then-rectify design is intuitive and useful: virtual re-shot views estimate semantic ambiguity, while nearby low-uncertainty objects provide contextual anchors for refining uncertain captions.
The evaluation is broad, covering SceneFun3D, FunGraph3D, Replica, pose-noise stress tests, ablations, human assessment, runtime considerations, and a physical robot demonstration.

Results are consistently favorable. In particular, the GPT variant improves object recall on both real-world benchmarks, while the open-weight LLaVA variant remains competitive or superior to prior work, suggesting that gains are not solely due to GPT-4o.

The Replica human evaluation complements recall-based automated metrics with node and edge precision, duplicate counts, three annotators, and substantial inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' kappa 0.76).

Ablations show large degradation without re-shot verification and smaller but consistent losses without RAG, spatially informed retrieval, or concatenated visual evidence. The method is clearly presented, and the figures effectively communicate the pipeline.
weaknesses: The re-shot uncertainty estimator is insufficiently validated as an uncertainty measure. The paper does not report calibration, error-detection AUROC, correlation with caption correctness, or comparisons against simpler confidence and view-consistency baselines. It assumes the re-shot caption is reliable, although the rendered point cloud is reconstructed from the same finite observations and cannot recover genuinely unseen or missing surfaces.

Several central implementation details are underspecified, including point-cloud rendering and visibility computation, caption clustering, consensus-caption construction, the final reliability score, dynamic nearest-neighbor matching, and the thresholding procedure. The fixed top-50% anchor choice is not justified or analyzed, limiting reproducibility.

The main comparison does not cleanly isolate the proposed contribution. RAG-3DSG simultaneously changes object mapping, downsampling, edge construction, relation categories, prompting, and foundation models. Component ablations are performed only on Replica under a different GPT-4o-based semantic-assignment evaluation, rather than on the two primary benchmarks. Comparisons with the cited viewpoint-selection methods would also strengthen the novelty case.

The principal benchmark reports recall only and maps free-form predicates using BERT similarity, which can obscure false positives and mapping errors. No confidence intervals, repeated-run variation, or significance tests are provided despite relatively small sets of 20 and 24 scenes. The human study helps but does not fully specify the total number of evaluated units, and agreement is measured on only 100 units.

The real-robot section is qualitative and apparently limited to one facility. It reports neither downstream task success nor quantitative accuracy, latency, or failure rates. Thus, claims of deployment readiness, exceptional resilience, and hallucination-free graphs are stronger than the presented evidence supports.

Runtime reporting is incomplete: the paper gives a mapping-stage example and approximate API cost but not end-to-end runtime, per-module latency, memory use, or full hardware specifications for both variants. No code or explicit artifact-release statement is provided, and prompts are deferred to supplementary material not included here.

The approach remains offline and depends on accurate RGB-D reconstruction, external foundation models, and semantic anchors that may themselves be wrong. Error propagation from an incorrect low-uncertainty anchor and sensitivity to severe missing geometry or domain shift are not examined.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant failure mode in open-vocabulary 3D scene-graph construction: inconsistent semantics caused by occlusion and restricted input viewpoints. Treating the submission as Algorithms/General, the proposed diagnose-then-rectify pipeline is intuitive and pertinent to embodied vision.

Rendering object point clouds from selected virtual viewpoints, comparing re-shot and passive captions, and using reliable neighboring objects as contextual anchors form a coherent system. The view score combines visibility, gravity alignment, and proximity to previously observed directions in a practically motivated way.

The evaluation is broader than that of many systems papers: it covers SceneFun3D, FunGraph3D, Replica, pose-noise stress tests, component ablations, runtime analysis, and a physical robot deployment. Ours-LLaVA is especially useful because it shows that the improvements are not limited to a proprietary VLM.

Results are promising. Ours-GPT improves object R@10 from 87.8 to 90.2 on SceneFun3D and from 79.1 to 83.0 on FunGraph3D; the Replica human study reports substantial node-precision gains over ConceptGraphs, while the ablations generally support the complementary roles of re-shooting, image concatenation, and retrieval.

The manuscript is well organized and visually clear. It includes equations, pseudocode, prompts, hyperparameter studies, deployment details, and a useful failure/recovery example in which an erroneous re-shot caption is corrected using the RGB crop and contextual anchor.
weaknesses: The uncertainty estimator is insufficiently specified and justified. The number k of passive captions is not stated, while the described passive variant uses only three crops and the method applies K-means with K=3. If k=3, clusters can degenerate to singletons and selecting the cluster with the highest mean similarity becomes close to selecting the single caption most similar to the re-shot. Behavior when fewer than three valid views exist, initialization sensitivity, and evidence that the score is calibrated or predictive of actual errors are absent.

The method treats the re-shot caption as the reference used to measure reliability, although re-rendered partial point clouds can themselves be ambiguous or incorrect. The paper provides one recovery example, but no systematic analysis of re-shot error frequency, uncertainty calibration, anchor contamination, or cases in which an incorrect re-shot and incorrect passive captions agree confidently.

Several central algorithmic details remain ambiguous. The dynamic nearest-neighbor ratio is not formally defined; the main text and Algorithm 1 do not fully specify association and thresholding; the composite similarity adds semantic and spatial quantities without normalization or weighting; and the dimensional interpretation of the scale-adaptive voxel formula is unclear. Rendering settings and the exact number of captions are also omitted.

The comparison does not cleanly isolate the proposed algorithm from foundation-model and prompting differences. Ours-GPT uses GPT-4o, whereas baseline backbone/prompt parity is unclear. Ours-LLaVA helps, but a controlled comparison that applies identical segmentation, mapping, VLM/LLM, prompts, and relation taxonomy with and without each contribution is missing on the two principal benchmarks.

The edge evidence is not fully convincing. The method constrains outputs to eight canonical relations and uses few-shot prompting, while the paper claims an open-vocabulary scene graph and compares against systems with potentially different relation spaces. BERT-based mapping can conceal taxonomy mismatches, gains over OpenFunGraph are small or absent on several edge metrics, and no per-relation results or semantic-mapping sensitivity analysis is provided.

The ablation study is performed on Replica using GPT-4o as a semantic label assigner rather than the principal SceneFun3D/FunGraph3D protocol. There are no repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite stochastic K-means and generative-model calls. Thus it is difficult to determine whether smaller benchmark gains are robust.

The human study lacks the total number of rated units, uncertainty estimates, hypothesis tests, and sufficient detail about annotator blinding. Fleiss' kappa is computed on only 100 sampled units, and the rule treating examples such as 'wooden table' and 'brown desk' as equivalent appears overly permissive rather than strictly synonymous.

The real-robot evidence is limited to offline processing of one indoor facility. The reported 83.8% versus 65.6% node precision lacks sample counts and uncertainty, and no downstream navigation or manipulation success is measured. Consequently, claims of readiness for reliable or safety-critical deployment are substantially stronger than the evidence supports.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: no code or release commitment is stated; complete few-shot demonstrations are explicitly omitted; decoding settings, seeds, exact model/API versions, K-means settings, rendering parameters, evaluation matching details, and complete runtime/hardware measurements are missing. Overall, the idea and results are promising, but these methodological and evaluation ambiguities slightly outweigh the case for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in open-vocabulary 3D scene-graph construction: captions aggregated across occluded or constrained views can be semantically inconsistent and propagate errors into relationships.
The diagnose-then-rectify pipeline is intuitive. It combines virtual re-rendering, an agreement-based reliability score, contextual refinement, and edge generation in a coherent system.

The empirical coverage is broader than average: two real-world benchmarks, Replica experiments, component and hyperparameter ablations, pose-noise tests, human evaluation, runtime analysis, and a physical robot demonstration are included.

The reported object-recognition improvements are encouraging. Ours-LLaVA improves FunGraph3D object R@3 from OpenFunGraph's 70.7 to 73.6, while Ours-GPT reaches 75.0; the Replica human study also reports appreciably higher node precision.
The paper is generally well organized, and the supplementary material provides prompts, pseudocode, qualitative cases, and several implementation parameters.
weaknesses: Assuming the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the central technical claim is insufficiently validated. The proposed 'uncertainty' is merely CLIP-text agreement between a re-shot caption and passive captions. The paper never evaluates whether this score predicts actual errors through calibration, AUROC, risk-coverage, or comparisons with basic uncertainty alternatives such as caption disagreement, entropy, or VLM confidence.

The uncertainty construction itself is questionable. The method clusters the top-k caption similarities with K-means using K=3, while the described passive setting uses only three top views. In that apparent configuration, clustering can degenerate to nearly one sample per cluster, and choosing the cluster with the highest mean effectively selects the most agreeable caption while ignoring contradictory evidence. Neither k nor safeguards for small or degenerate clusters are adequately specified.

The ablations do not cleanly establish the claimed mechanism. Removing re-shot estimation changes downstream filtering and fusion behavior simultaneously, and 'w/o uncertainty' applies refinement to every object rather than replacing the proposed score with a competing uncertainty estimator. Consequently, the large degradation does not demonstrate that the proposed score is a sound ambiguity measure.

The 're-shot' operation cannot recover appearance that was never observed: it renders an incomplete, noisy, fused point cloud rather than acquiring a new RGB observation. Rendering details needed to assess or reproduce this step—point splatting, visibility computation, colors, camera intrinsics, hole handling, and treatment of unseen surfaces—are missing. Calling this active verification or an active photographer overstates what is an offline virtual-view selection procedure.

The object-level RAG contribution is technically modest: it injects the caption of the single nearest low-uncertainty object into a VLM prompt. It retrieves neither external knowledge nor multiple evidence records, and spatial proximity does not guarantee semantic relevance. Comparisons against stronger contextual baselines, semantic retrieval, graph-neighborhood reasoning, or equivalent non-RAG prompting are absent.

The main comparisons are confounded by different foundation models, mapping procedures, and edge prompts. Ours-GPT is presented as the headline system without an equivalently upgraded baseline, while the more comparable Ours-LLaVA does not outperform OpenFunGraph on any reported edge metric. Even Ours-GPT only ties FunGraph3D edge R@10 and improves some other edge results by small margins. No repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for stochastic/API-based inference.

The automated evaluation is under-specified. The exact mapping from free-form node captions to object ground truth is unclear, GPT-4o is itself used as a semantic assigner in the Replica ablation, and model/version, decoding, and reproducibility details are incomplete. This makes the reported gains difficult to audit independently.

The human evaluation reports precision and valid counts without total prediction counts, confidence intervals, per-method sampling details, or an analysis controlling for graph density. Edge precision can be increased by predicting fewer or easier edges. Agreement is measured on only 100 unspecified units, and the real-robot precision comparison gives no sample size or raw counts.

The real-world deployment evidence is too limited for the paper's strong reliability and readiness claims. It consists of an offline pipeline in one indoor facility, one qualitative visualization, and an incompletely documented human-precision result; there is no downstream navigation/manipulation evaluation, failure-rate analysis, latency demonstration on the robot, or safety study.

Several technical definitions need correction or clarification. The dynamic voxel formula is dimensionally inconsistent if both the base value and bounding-box diagonal are measured in meters; the fusion score combines semantic and spatial terms without defined normalization or gating; and a threshold of 0.45 is difficult to interpret for a sum whose apparent range is up to two. The pseudocode does not resolve these ambiguities.

The manuscript repeatedly uses conclusions stronger than the evidence supports, including 'exceptional resilience,' 'disproves the concern,' and readiness for reliable deployment. A single mild pose-noise setting—2 cm translation and 1 degree rotation—does not constitute an extreme geometric stress test, and the limitations of incomplete geometry, contextual bias, API dependence, and offline processing are not discussed adequately.

strengths: Evaluated as an Algorithms/General submission because no contribution type is explicitly declared. The diagnose-then-rectify pipeline is a coherent and useful contribution: virtual re-shot views expose cross-view semantic disagreement, while uncertainty-guided retrieval uses nearby reliable objects to refine ambiguous nodes.

The paper addresses an important failure mode in open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs—semantic corruption from occlusion and constrained viewpoints—and provides intuitive case studies showing how the proposed components can correct such errors.

The empirical evaluation is broad: 44 real-world benchmark scenes across SceneFun3D and FunGraph3D, eight Replica scenes, pose-noise stress tests, human evaluation, runtime and cost analysis, and a physical robot deployment. Both GPT-4o and local LLaVA variants are reported.

Results are consistently competitive. Ours-GPT improves object recall over OpenFunGraph on both benchmarks, while the LLaVA variant also obtains strong results. Human evaluation reports sizable gains in node precision (0.82 versus 0.68/0.58) and edge precision (0.91 versus 0.82/0.85), with substantial inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' kappa 0.76).

The ablations are informative: removing re-shots, RAG, image concatenation, or spatially meaningful retrieval reduces performance, and additional analyses cover retrieval size, uncertainty guidance, voxel size, merging threshold, point density, and viewpoint-scoring factors.

The manuscript is generally clear and visually effective, and it provides useful engineering details including hardware, synchronization, computation distribution, prompts, pseudocode, API cost, and runtime.
weaknesses: The proposed uncertainty score is semantic agreement with a generated re-shot caption rather than a demonstrated or calibrated estimate of correctness. The paper does not directly evaluate uncertainty quality through calibration, error-detection AUROC, risk-coverage curves, or accuracy as a function of the score. Consequently, the central claim that the method reliably 'knows what it does not know' is only indirectly supported.

Several key choices remain underspecified or heuristic: the number of passive captions k is not clearly fixed, yet KMeans uses K=3; the top 50% split between reliable and uncertain objects is arbitrary; and sensitivity to this split is absent. If only three captions are used, three-way clustering can become degenerate. Renderer settings and some few-shot prompt demonstrations are also omitted despite the claim of complete prompt templates.

A virtual re-shot cannot recover genuinely unobserved texture or geometry—it only rerenders the fused, potentially incomplete point cloud. Thus, claims that the method breaks dependence on finite observations, eliminates occlusion, or provides an effectively unconstrained verification space are overstated. The included failure case where a re-shot becomes a 'white candle' illustrates this limitation.

The automated comparison is not completely controlled for foundation-model capacity and protocol choices. The strongest variant uses proprietary GPT-4o, while baselines may use different semantic backbones; the method also constrains edges to eight relations despite describing the framework as open-vocabulary. Backbone-matched results and the node-plus-ConceptGraphs-edge variant help, but a stronger comparison using identical mapping, VLM, prompts, and relation vocabulary would isolate the algorithmic contribution better.

Reported gains lack confidence intervals, per-scene statistical tests, or repeated-run variance. The human study covers only 100 units for agreement, does not clearly report the complete number of rated samples, and compares against only ConceptGraphs variants rather than the strongest OpenFunGraph baseline.

The robot evaluation is offline, teleoperated, apparently limited to one facility, and does not measure success on an actual downstream navigation or manipulation task. It supports physical feasibility, but statements about readiness for reliable or safety-critical deployment are stronger than the evidence warrants.

Reproducibility is limited by dependence on proprietary GPT-4o, incomplete prompt details, and no stated code or evaluation-annotation release. The paper would also benefit from an explicit limitations discussion covering API/model drift, partial reconstructions, erroneous semantic anchors, and propagation of VLM hallucinations.
